item.title: Scientists just found dinosaur blood that survived 115 million years
item.description: Scientists have discovered chemically confirmed traces of ancient blood inside 115-million-year-old dinosaur bones, challenging assumptions about how long biological molecules can survive. The extraordinary preservation could unlock new clues about dinosaur physiology and even help scientists search for ancient life elsewhere in the universe.

item.title: Five-inch-long beetle larvae are quietly destroying blueberry roots
item.description: Scientists have solved a mystery surrounding destructive beetles attacking blueberry bushes in North Carolina, identifying a species whose massive larvae can grow up to five inches long and destroy plant roots. Although farmers have reported damage for more than a decade, the insects responsible remained unidentified until researchers used DNA analysis to uncover the culprit.

item.title: Don't miss: Meteor showers, fireballs, and a supermoon light up November's night sky
item.description: November's night sky is packed with celestial wonders, from bright meteor fireballs and a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter to a spectacular supermoon. Meanwhile, NASA's Voyager 1 is making history by becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.

item.title: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
item.description: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that some dead stars can grow far more massive than scientists once thought possible. Computer simulations show that powerful magnetic fields could allow white dwarfs to reach 2.4 times the mass of the Sun, dramatically exceeding a famous limit that has stood for decades. item.title: Scientists discover that a clogged filter could revolutionize oil refining
item.description: Scientists have developed a remarkable new membrane that separates crude oil at room temperature, using the oil itself to create microscopic filtration channels. The breakthrough could cut refining energy consumption by nearly 32%, carbon emissions by almost 38%, and operating costs by 36%, potentially transforming one of the world's most energy-intensive industries.

item.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear.

item.title: Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation
item.description: Scientists have solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered a hidden immune system defense that protects healthy cells from the very inflammation meant to fight infections. The surprising discovery could lead to new approaches for treating cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions involving excessive inflammation.

item.title: Scientists may have finally explained why our brains and bodies are cross-wired
item.description: Scientists propose that the brain’s mysterious cross-wiring, which connects each hemisphere to the opposite side of the body, may have originated more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of ancient fish. Rather than evolving for a specific advantage, this unusual arrangement may simply be a legacy of evolution building new brain circuits on an ancient foundation.

item.title: Permanent daylight saving time has a dark side, scientists warn
item.description: A new study warns that permanent daylight saving time could force American children to make at least 2 billion additional school commutes in darkness, potentially increasing safety risks and disrupting their biological clocks. Researchers found that fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.

item.title: MIT scientists break a 20-year rule and unlock never-before-seen crystal structures

The breakthrough could lead to a new generation of designer materials with unusual properties and applications in electronics, medicine, and energy.

item.description: A single gene-editing treatment could someday protect against heart disease, high cholesterol, and other common conditions for decades, potentially replacing lifelong medications. item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03171-3 Brains are resilient. Harnessing their self-protective mechanisms might help to prevent or slow the progression of this neurodegenerative condition.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03167-z Most Parkinson’s therapies aim to reduce the motor-control symptoms that the disease triggers. But stem-cell transplants in the brain could alter the disease at a more fundamental level.

item.title: Progress accelerates in Parkinson’s treatments
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03165-1 Researchers are reporting encouraging results for a disease that affects millions of people worldwide.

item.title: Ecosystems depend on people: don’t abandon them

item.title: Fruit, flies and getting frisky: how food odours trigger sexual arousal
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03271-0 Males of a Drosophila species that thrives on a particular fruit need the smell of food to begin courtship. This environmental cue acts on defined mating circuits in the brain.

item.title: Six highlights from Parkinson’s disease research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03172-2 Targeting a new network, addressing gait issues and other advances from recent studies.

item.title: Cutting-edge technique uncovers how the spine’s shock absorbers bear load
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03264-z An exciting imaging approach reveals how discs of soft tissue in the spine respond to compressive force at the micrometre and nanometre scales.

item.title: Epileptic seizures nearly vanish after people receive experimental gene therapy in their brains
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03566-2 A clinical trial in three people tested a combination of gene-laden viruses and a drug.

item.title: A death sentence for ‘sloppy’ cancers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03269-8 The process of making protein from RNA can go awry in cancer cells. This malfunction might be harnessed to create an effective gene-therapy tool that targets tumours.

item.title: Faint exoplanets detected using computational approach to remove glare from stars
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03295-6 An image-processing framework for detecting exoplanets directly has been developed. The technique overcomes the telescope-stability barrier that has limited previous methods, reveals fainter exoplanets than other approaches can detect and could make imaging exo-Earths easier for future observatories.

item.title: People’s social networks can be unintentionally reshaped during randomized interventions
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03267-w A re-examination of a randomized controlled trial for a health-advice intervention reveals ripple effects and altered relationships in communities in rural Honduras.

item.title: Fine-tuning brain stimulation to fight Parkinson’s disease
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03168-y Neuroscientists are developing a new type of brain implant that will decode every movement and symptom of people with this neurodegenerative condition, seeking better ways to ease symptoms.

item.title: Mysterious anthrax outbreak kills hippos in Africa — raising concerns for human spread
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03580-4 The latest cases, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, come as the country grapples with ongoing Ebola and cholera outbreaks.

item.title: When humans disappear, biodiversity takes a surprising turn
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03505-1 For decades, conservation has worried about the risks of too many people. In some places, depopulation is the real threat.

item.title: Could chemicals contribute to Parkinson’s?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03170-4 Researchers and advocates point to pollutants as a trigger for the neurodegenerative condition.

item.title: Replacing the neurons that Parkinson’s destroys
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03166-0 After decades of work, researchers have begun trialling transplants of dopamine neurons into people with the neurodegenerative disease — with early signs of success.

item.title: Why are we conscious? Nature investigates the theories
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03413-4 Scientists have yet to reveal how the human brain produces the subjective experience we perceive as consciousness, but research has pushed the field in exciting directions.

item.title: Infrared image detectors grown directly on read-out chips
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03420-5 A film of lead sulfide — an infrared-sensitive semiconductor — has been grown directly on a circuit that can read out the material’s electrical signal through an approach called monolithic in situ integration. This brings material growth and electronic integration together into a single step. The resulting image sensor show

item.title: A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8 A two-dimensional reticular triaxial woven network material is constructed by incorporating C3-symmetric macrocycles into a triangular weave pattern, enabling an extra topological dimension to be used for the construction of functional materials.

item.title: Accelerating commercialization and deployment of indoor photovoltaics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11133-y Recent progress in photovoltaics has been investigated to translate state-of-the-art cells in the laboratory into deployable products suited to real indoor conditions, focusing on wide-bandgap absorbers, reduced non-radiative voltage losses and reshaping module design.

item.title: In vivo CAR-T double knockout screen maps synergistic antitumour gene pairs
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10956-z Using high-throughput in vivo CAR-T double knockout screening, synergistic gene combinations to improve CAR-T cell therapy are revealed.

item.title: Observation of prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11225-9 A programmable neutral-atom quantum simulator is used to explore quench dynamics in spin models with up to 180 qubits, revealing prethermal dynamical phase transitions and resonant melting.

item.title: Ecological and social cues orchestrate concerted courtship in Drosophila
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11209-9 In Drosophila erecta, food odours initiate male sexual arousal, which is subsequently reinforced by the visual motion of other courting flies, creating a multisensory mechanism that synchronizes courtship in groups when conditions are favourable for reproduction.

item.title: An AI-native experimental laboratory for autonomous biomolecular operations
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11228-6 AutoDNA is an artificial intelligence (AI)-native autonomous biomolecular engineering laboratory targeting multi-objective experiments across diverse instruments, realizing the co-evolution of AI and the automation system within an end-to-end multi-user framework.

item.title: Multimodal X-ray imaging reveals hierarchical fibre mechanics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11148-5 The X-ray visualization platform TomoSAXS, demonstrated here on intervertebral spinal discs, can visualize nanoscale to macroscale mechanics in intact biological organs and fibrous materials.

item.title: Towards observing interstitial hydrogen in solution in metal lattices
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11238-4 Using deuterium as a proxy for hydrogen, atom probe tomography provides experimental evidence for interstitial hydrogen in solid solution across different FCC phases, consistent with theoretical predictions of hydrogen affinity, revealing hydrogen partitioning in structural alloys.

item.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11177-0 Multi-omic analyses of cells from patients with glioblastoma (GB) provide insight into the role of non-genetic cellular plasticity in disease progression, showing that state stability in GB cells is controlled by a network of interacting activators and repressors.

item.title: Comprehensive mapping of essential-gene interactions in M. tuberculosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11212-0 A high-throughput CRISPR-interference platform allows the mapping of interactions between essential genes in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, revealing many previously unknown genetic interactions and providing insight into gene function and drug–target relationships that could enable the development of new therapies for tubercu

item.title: Conjugation-regulated self-assembled molecules for tandem solar cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11226-8 Rationally engineered molecular spatial conjugation is used for the formation of highly ordered, conformal self-assembled molecules, enabling the fabrication of high-performance perovskite/silicon tandem solar cells.

item.title: Hard X-ray attosecond metrology
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11245-5 Metrology techniques are developed to characterize and control attosecond hard X-ray pulses, directly measuring a 170-attosecond duration and enabling ultrafast studies of electronic dynamics in quantum systems.

item.title: Cancer-selective gene circuits via intrinsic ribosomal frameshifting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11200-4 Codon-pair-dependent ribosomal frameshifting is a feature of translational dysregulation in cancer cells.

item.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11198-9 Genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals are analysed, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which alternative archaeological and linguistic models for the origin and spread of Celtic fit reconstructed demographic histories.

item.title: Venousization enables angiogenesis in the absence of VEGFR signalling
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11224-w Longitudinal tracking of endothelial cells shows they can adapt to loss of VEGFR2 and form new functional vessels, challenging conventional views of the essential role of VEGF receptors in angiogenesis and providing insight into resistance to anti-VEGF therapies.

item.title: The neural basis of flavour–nutrient learning
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11229-5 A dopamine pathway to the basolateral amygdala is necessary for associating nutrients with flavours.

item.title: Nectin-4 mediates rubella virus entry in airway and placental cells
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11248-2 Nectin-4 is identified as a pivotal host entry receptor for respiratory transmission and early placental infection of rubella virus.

item.title: Aggression experience and observation drive shared behavioural and neural changes
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11217-9 Aggression experience and observation recruit a brain-wide network of excitatory, inhibitory and valence signals, and changes to this activation pattern predict a shared adaptive behaviour-control policy in a new aggression context.

item.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11236-6 Gene network analysis shows how mutations in diverse genes associated with autism spectrum disorder can converge to exert shared effects, with X-linked transcription factor ZFX emerging as a key protective factor in the female brain.

item.title: The deep Earth origin of the Great Unconformity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11156-5 Continental-scale uplift and subsidence associated with long-wavelength dynamic topography due to mantle convection drove the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity.

item.title: Twist-angle-dependent quantum phase diagrams in moiré bilayer MoTe 2
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11274-0 Twist-angle-dependent studies of moiré bilayer MoTe2 reveal a transition from fractional topological states to correlated insulators and superconductivity, linking topology, symmetry breaking and magnetism in moiré quantum materials.

item.title: An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11210-2 structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model pre-trained on 21 million sequence–structure pairs, learns multimodal representations that improve secondary and tertiary structure prediction, functional inference and zero-shot generalization across diverse RNA families.

item.title: Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11243-7 Viral–bacterial synergy accelerates algal bloom collapse by enhancing virus-induced mortality, driven by Alteromonas chemoattraction and co-infection, revealing a previously unrecognized mortality agent that influences oceanic carbon cycling .

item.title: A conserved flowering-time module underlies double-season cropping
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11187-y The genomic footprints of 80 years of modern breeding in China are traced using representative cultivars, demonstrating how precision genome editing can be used to reconstruct adaptive modules for climate-resilient crop design.

item.title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11220-0 Gut microbial single-nucleotide variants across 10,781 individuals reveal 940 associations that link strain-level genetic variation to 69 host traits, with structural analyses pinpointing host phenotype-associated variants, providing a base pair-resolution resource for mechanistic hypothesis generation.

item.title: A spatiotemporal cancer cell trajectory underlies glioblastoma heterogeneity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11234-8 A deep single-cell and spatial multi-omic atlas of human glioblastoma is generated, pairing transcriptomic, epigenomic and genomic profiling, and tracing glioblastoma tumour heterogeneity to a stereotyped and spatially patterned trajectory of cancer cells.

item.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
item.description: Nature, Published online: 04 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11213-z A new physics-based method combining the use of automatic differentiation to optimize millions of model parameters with a flexible physical model is described for starlight subtraction from real, on-sky coronagraphic images to greatly improve sensitivity.

item.title: The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD
item.description: A surprising new discovery suggests that fear may cause the brain to blur the line between danger and safety rather than distinguish them more clearly. By observing brain activity in mice using augmented reality, scientists found that memories of threatening and harmless environments began to overlap, potentially allowing faster responses to danger. This "better safe than sorry" survival mechanism

item.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
item.description: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.

item.title: Scientists identify two overlooked skills that predict reading success
item.description: A massive new study reveals that intelligence plays a surprisingly limited role in children's reading success, while visual processing showed no meaningful connection at all. Instead, the strongest predictors are sound recognition, vocabulary, and background knowledge, offering new clues about how to help struggling readers.

item.title: All 5 genetic “letters” of DNA and RNA discovered in a 4.5-billion-year-old asteroid
item.description: Scientists have discovered all five essential nucleobases used in DNA and RNA in pristine samples from asteroid Ryugu, revealing that key ingredients for life existed in space billions of years ago. The remarkable finding adds to growing evidence from other asteroids and meteorites that these molecules were widespread throughout the early Solar System.

item.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened
item.description: Europe’s Hera spacecraft has captured its first clear view of two asteroids involved in NASA’s historic 2022 experiment to redirect a potentially dangerous space rock. Now approaching the pair, Hera will investigate the mysterious aftermath of the collision and uncover why the asteroid shifted far more than scientists predicted.

item.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
item.description: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.

item.title: Large Hadron Collider reveals evidence of Big Bang matter in surprisingly small collisions
item.description: Scientists at CERN's Large Hadron Collider have uncovered compelling new evidence that even relatively small atomic collisions can recreate the extraordinary state of matter that filled the universe moments after the Big Bang. Known as quark-gluon plasma, this exotic substance forms at temperatures more than 100,000 times hotter than the center of the Sun, causing ordinary particles to break apart

item.title: Scientists just found a loophole that could let black holes split in two
item.description: Scientists have discovered a possible loophole in the laws that normally prevent black holes from splitting apart, suggesting that extremely fast-spinning black holes might divide into two. The surprising finding raises the possibility of an entirely new black hole phenomenon that future telescopes could potentially detect.

item.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps

item.title: Whence dragons?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03277-8 The ecology and evolution of winged legendary beasts, and monkeys that show their behinds to their buddies, in this week’s pick from the Nature archive.

item.title: Research bonuses need clear and fair rules
item.description: Nature, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03562-6 Research bonuses need clear and fair rules

item.title: IceCube detects ghost particles with 10 billion times the energy of solar neutrinos
item.description: Mysterious particles called neutrinos constantly stream through our bodies, and scientists are now detecting incredibly powerful versions arriving from distant cosmic sources using a massive observatory buried in Antarctic ice. These elusive “ghost particles” could hold extraordinary clues about the Big Bang, extreme cosmic events, and some of the universe’s greatest mysteries.

item.title: Scientists discover that some “unhealthy” diets can boost cancer immunotherapy in mice
item.description: In a surprising discovery, scientists found that certain diets associated with obesity can make cancer immunotherapy more effective in mice, challenging traditional assumptions about diet and cancer treatment. The findings suggest that the secret may lie in how food interacts with gut bacteria to strengthen the immune system's response to cancer.

item.title: NASA reveals a haunting skull hidden in Antarctica’s ice
item.description: NASA satellites have captured an eerie, skull-shaped formation on a remote Antarctic island, but its haunting appearance conceals a troubling warning about melting glaciers. Unusually warm winter temperatures have exposed large areas of dark ice, potentially accelerating future melting and gradually transforming the skull's ghostly features.

item.title: 30,000-year-old DNA reveals Ice Age Europeans were far more connected than we thought
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising DNA evidence that Europeans living more than 30,000 years ago were connected across vast distances, challenging the idea that ancient populations remained largely isolated. Genetic clues from human remains and cave sediments reveal prehistoric migration, long-lasting communities, and survival through the harshest conditions of the Ice Age.

item.title: NASA's Hubble and Webb discover ancient worlds that remember their past
item.description: NASA’s Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have uncovered surprising clues about the solar system’s origins by studying 27 tiny, distant objects beyond Neptune. Scientists discovered that these ancient building blocks of planets have remained remarkably unchanged for billions of years, while their unexpected sizes and numbers challenge existing theories of planet formation.

item.title: Common pesticide linked to 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson’s disease
item.description: A UCLA study found that long-term exposure to a common pesticide was linked to more than 2.5 times the risk of Parkinson's disease. Scientists also uncovered how the chemical damages brain cells and identified a promising way to protect them.

item.title: Scientists shrink Archimedes’ screw to the size of a single molecule
item.description: Scientists have built a groundbreaking molecular motor that spins in either direction using electricity, inspired by a machine invented more than 2,000 years ago. Even more remarkably, its rotation can boost electrical conductivity by up to 100 times, potentially transforming the future of molecular electronics.

item.title: Scientists use sound waves to deliver a new attack on deadly brain cancer
item.description: Scientists at the University of Virginia have developed a promising new strategy to fight glioblastoma, one of the deadliest and most difficult-to-treat forms of brain cancer. Their experimental approach combines focused ultrasound, tiny nanoparticles, and genetic molecules called microRNAs to attack multiple cancer-driving genes simultaneously.

item.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt could rewrite the story of human origins
item.description: A 17- to 18-million-year-old ape fossil discovered in Egypt is challenging long-held beliefs about where the ancestors of humans and other modern apes first evolved. Scientists now suspect that North Africa and the Middle East, rather than East Africa, may have been the cradle of modern ape evolution.

item.title: Scientists say a forgotten particle may explain why the universe exists
item.description: A mysterious particle overlooked for decades may hold the key to why matter survived the Big Bang, allowing stars, planets, and life to exist. Scientists believe this forgotten neutrino reshaped the early universe and may have left detectable gravitational wave signals that could help unlock the cosmos’s deepest mysteries.

item.title: Scientists discover the hidden “muscles” trees use to straighten themselves
item.description: Scientists have discovered that trees can sense their own shape and straighten their trunks using specialized wood that acts like opposing muscles. This remarkable ability helps trees maintain their posture and could lead to stronger forests, better timber, and more resilient crops.

item.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
item.description: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.

item.title: Scientists discover metals that defy the deep freeze at -424°F
item.description: Scientists have discovered a surprising mechanism that allows certain metals to resist cracking at temperatures as low as -253°C (-424°F), when similar materials typically become dangerously brittle. Instead of breaking, two experimental alloys reorganize their internal structures, creating new ways to absorb stress and remain flexible.

item.title: 75,000-year-old Neanderthal may have been killed by a spear aimed at the heart
item.description: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been killed by a wooden spear deliberately aimed at the heart, revealing rare evidence of prehistoric violence. A circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests the weapon pierced the chest and caused a rapidly fatal injury. Surprisingly, the same individual had survived an earlier devastating facial injury, suggesting other Neanderthals provided care

item.title: Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken
item.description: Scientists have discovered a bizarre bacterial defense system that works almost completely backward from anything seen before. Unlike typical bacterial immune systems that keep a deadly toxin under control until a virus attacks, this unusual mechanism waits until an infection begins before producing the DNA that switches on its lethal weapon. The infected bacterium then destroys itself, preventing

item.title: A surprising vitamin A discovery is changing what scientists know about vision
item.description: Scientists at Johns Hopkins University have uncovered a surprising process that helps humans develop sharp vision before birth, challenging decades of assumptions about how the eye forms. Using miniature human retinas grown in the lab, researchers discovered that a vitamin A derivative and thyroid hormones work together to shape the foveola, the tiny region at the center of the retina responsible

item.title: Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang
item.description: Scientists have recreated a primordial state of matter from the dawn of the universe by colliding oxygen nuclei at nearly the speed of light. The surprising results show that this exotic substance can form in smaller, lower-energy collisions than previously demonstrated, challenging the known boundaries of early-universe physics.

item.title: A simple blood test could reveal Alzheimer’s risk 10 years before symptoms
item.description: A major international study found that a simple blood test could help predict Alzheimer’s-related cognitive decline years before symptoms appear, with the highest-risk individuals facing a 38% chance of impairment within five years and an estimated 78% chance within 10 years. Scientists believe the discovery could pave the way for earlier intervention and future treatments designed to prevent Alzh

item.title: Physicists created a tiny universe and watched time emerge without a clock
item.description: Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that t

item.title: The asteroid killed the dinosaurs. Why did crocodiles survive?
item.description: Scientists may have solved a 66-million-year-old mystery: how crocodiles survived the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs. A sweeping analysis of fossils and ancient climates suggests that their preference for warm environments placed them in tropical refuges that remained habitable even after the catastrophic impact.

item.title: Hubble reveals a stunning twist in how the universe emerged from darkness
item.description: A surprising discovery by astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope is challenging a leading explanation for how the early universe emerged from a dense fog of hydrogen roughly 13 billion years ago. Scientists once believed powerful winds from exploding stars helped radiation escape galaxies and clear that cosmic fog, but new observations reveal that these winds actually block radiation instead

item.title: Scientists reveal a hidden snakebite crisis killing up to 513,000 people a year
item.description: A startling new study suggests that venomous snakebites are killing far more people worldwide than official statistics indicate, with an estimated 274,000 to 513,000 deaths every year. Researchers found that as many as 7 million people could suffer snake envenoming annually, while more than 800,000 survivors are left with long-term disabilities.

item.title: Astronauts just gave the International Space Station a powerful upgrade
item.description: Two astronauts completed a 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk to install a new solar array on the International Space Station, bringing NASA one step closer to a major power upgrade. Once the final array is installed on November 5, the station will have up to 30% more available power, supporting critical operations and its eventual controlled deorbit.

item.title: A mysterious star system just 16 light-years away may be hiding habitable planets
item.description: Astronomers have solved a 170-year-old planetary mystery in a nearby two-star system, discovering that a mysterious wobble was caused by stellar activity rather than a giant planet. Although Jupiter-sized worlds have been ruled out in key regions, smaller, potentially habitable planets could still be waiting to be discovered just 16 light-years from Earth.

item.title: Scientists discover mysterious seahorse lookalikes that no one has ever seen alive
item.description: Scientists have discovered that three bizarre deep-sea fish that look exactly like seahorses actually belong to a separate evolutionary group, proving that nature created the same unusual body shape more than once. Nicknamed "sea muppets," these elusive creatures are known from just seven specimens, and no one has ever seen one alive.

item.title: Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
item.description: A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not es

item.title: NASA discovers Jupiter’s invisible shield is more complex than Earth’s
item.description: NASA’s Juno spacecraft has discovered that Jupiter uses a surprisingly complex system of powerful plasma waves and multiple shock regions to defend against the solar wind. The findings reveal major differences between Jupiter and Earth and could help scientists understand the enormous shock waves produced by exploding stars.

item.title: Einstein's equations may explain the universe without dark energy
item.description: Mathematicians have uncovered what they argue is a fundamental flaw in the standard model of the universe, potentially challenging the need for dark energy. Their calculations suggest that the mathematical framework used to describe cosmic expansion is inherently unstable and that the universe could accelerate naturally under Einstein's original theory of gravity. item.title: 128,000-year-old ice in Tibet could rewrite climate history
item.description: Ancient ice discovered high in Tibet may be more than 128,000 years old, preserving an extraordinary record of Earth's climate that scientists previously thought had been lost. The discovery reveals a rare glimpse into the last ice age and could reshape our understanding of how glaciers survive dramatic changes in global climate.
